primer.eth_p_world.title: A kingdom in the mountains
primer.eth_p_world.text: You were born in highland Ethiopia, a Christian kingdom surrounded by Muslim sultanates and pagan peoples. Christianity arrived here back in the fourth century, under King Ezana of Aksum, earlier than in much of Europe. The ruler bears the title negusa nagast, "king of kings". The highlands, towering over the hot plains, protect the country but also cut it off from the world: Europe knows it only through legends of Prester John, a mighty Christian priest-king.
primer.eth_p_world_zagwe.title: The Zagwe kings
primer.eth_p_world_zagwe.text: The Zagwe dynasty from the mountains of Lasta is in power. Its most famous king is Lalibela, who ruled from about 1181 to 1221: at his command a whole city of churches was carved into red rock, a "New Jerusalem" for those who cannot reach the real one. The Zagwe do not claim descent from Solomon, and so many consider their rule illegitimate. Ties with Egypt, which sends the head of the church, the abuna, hold firm, and Ethiopian pilgrims still make their way to Jerusalem.
primer.eth_p_world_solomonic.title: The house of Solomon
primer.eth_p_world_solomonic.text: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak of Amhara seized power and proclaimed himself a descendant of King Solomon, founding the Solomonic dynasty. His grandson Amda Seyon (1314–1344) crushed the Muslim sultanate of Ifat and brought many southern lands under his rule. Around the same time the Kebra Nagast, "the Glory of the Kings", was compiled: the story of how Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark of the Covenant from Jerusalem. Kings Dawit and Yeshaq carry on the wars against their Muslim neighbours.
primer.eth_p_world_zara.title: Zara Yaqob and Eleni
primer.eth_p_world_zara.text: King Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) is a stern reformer: he was crowned at Aksum, fought heresy and sorcery, built churches and wrote theological books himself. His widow, the wise Queen Eleni, shapes court affairs for decades and is the first to seek an alliance with Christian Portugal. From 1520 to 1526 a Portuguese embassy lives at the court of King Lebna Dengel, and the priest Francisco Álvares writes down everything he sees. But in the east the Muslim sultanate of Adal is growing stronger.
primer.eth_p_world_gran.title: The war with Gragn
primer.eth_p_world_gran.text: A terrible time. Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of Adal, whom the Christians call Gragn, "the Left-handed", routed King Lebna Dengel's army at Shimbra Kure in 1529 and swept across the country. His men, armed with Turkish matchlocks, burn churches and monasteries and have sacked even Aksum; many Christians turn Muslim to survive. The king died a fugitive in 1540. In 1541 four hundred Portuguese musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama landed to help, and in 1543 Gragn fell in battle at Wayna Daga.
primer.eth_p_world_oromo.title: The Oromo and the Jesuits
primer.eth_p_world_oromo.text: The country is healing from the war with Gragn, but a new force is pressing up from the south: the Oromo, cattle herders who migrate north in waves and settle the emptied lands. Kings Galawdewos, Sarsa Dengel and Susenyos spend nearly their whole lives on campaign. Jesuit missionaries arrive from Portugal; in 1622 King Susenyos declared himself a Catholic and tried to convert the country, setting off revolts and bloodshed. There is still no capital: the court roams with its huge camp.
primer.eth_p_world_gondar.title: The castles of Gondar
primer.eth_p_world_gondar.text: In 1632 Susenyos, worn down by rebellion, restored the old faith and abdicated. His son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits and around 1636 founded a permanent capital near Lake Tana: Gondar, where stone castles with towers are rising. After centuries of a wandering court, the kingdom finally has a city. The old church triumphs, and ties with Catholic Europe are cut for a long time, though trade with Muslim neighbours and Egypt goes on.
primer.eth_p_world_harar_adal.title: Capital of Adal
primer.eth_p_world_harar_adal.text: Harar is the chief city of the sultanate of Adal, the Muslim rival of the Christian kingdom. The city is full of scholars, merchants and preachers, and many here call for holy war against "the king of the unbelievers". In 1520 Sultan Abu Bakr moved his capital here, and soon afterwards the young imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim took power. From 1529 his armies, armed with Turkish guns, sweep across the highlands, and booty, captives and news of victories pour into Harar.
primer.eth_p_world_harar_nur.title: Emir Nur's wall
primer.eth_p_world_harar_nur.text: After Imam Ahmad's death in 1543 his widow Bati Del Wambara called for revenge, and her new husband, Emir Nur, defeated and killed the Christian king Galawdewos in 1559. Around 1560 the emir also ringed Harar with a wall pierced by five gates. But Adal is exhausted, and the Oromo are advancing from the west and south, cutting the city off from its pastures and roads. In 1577 the sultan moved his capital to the distant oasis of Aussa, and Harar lives on by trade, faith and its own emirs.
primer.eth_p_society.title: King, nobles, ploughmen
primer.eth_p_society.text: At the top stands the negusa nagast, the "king of kings", surrounded by his court, commanders and clergy. Nobles receive gult from the king, the right to collect dues from villages, and govern them as long as the king's favour lasts. The backbone of the country is the peasants with their hereditary land, rist. The church and the monasteries own vast estates. Lower down are the craftsmen, whom people avoid: smiths, potters and tanners are suspected of sorcery. Lower still are the barya, servants in bondage.
primer.eth_p_society_slave.title: Barya
primer.eth_p_society_slave.text: You belong to the barya, servants in bondage. Most of them are captives from the pagan lands to the south and west, seized in raids or bought from traders. Church law forbids selling baptised Christians to people of another faith, but the rule is broken, and caravans lead people away to the coast and on to Arabia. In noble households the bonded fetch water, grind grain and herd cattle; many are baptised and in time become almost part of the family. Setting a servant free is counted a good deed.
primer.eth_p_society_peasant.title: Holder of rist
primer.eth_p_society_peasant.text: You come from peasants with hereditary land, rist. Rist is a right to land inherited through any ancestor, on the father's side or the mother's, so everyone remembers their genealogy many generations back and goes to law over boundaries endlessly. Fields are ploughed with a wooden maresha drawn by a pair of oxen and sown with teff, barley and sorghum. Part of the harvest, honey and livestock go to the lord who holds the gult and to the church, and passing soldiers, or the royal camp if it halts nearby, must be fed as well.
primer.eth_p_society_noble.title: The king's favour
primer.eth_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a family of the court nobility. Nobles receive gult from the king, the right to collect dues from villages, along with titles such as ras or bitwoded. But all of it is the king's favour, not an inheritance: a man who falls from grace can lose his lands in a single day. Noble sons grow up in the royal camp, learning to ride, to fight with the spear and to follow court etiquette. The most dangerous nobility is royal blood: for generations the king's male relatives were held captive on the sheer mountain of Amba Geshen so they could not raise a revolt.
primer.eth_p_society_harar.title: City of emirs
primer.eth_p_society_harar.text: Harar has an order of its own. An emir or sultan rules, flanked by the ulama, scholars of faith and law, and by the sheikhs of Sufi brotherhoods, whose word weighs as much as the emir's. The city's wealth is in the hands of merchants trading with Zeila, Arabia and the highlands. Craftsmen — weavers, smiths, bookbinders — live in their own quarters. Outside the walls peasants work the land, and in the houses slaves brought from the south do the serving. Every townsman belongs to the community of his quarter and his mosque.
primer.eth_p_birth.title: Forty days
primer.eth_p_birth.text: A midwife and the neighbour women delivered you, and by custom your mother rests for several weeks, eating thick genfo porridge with clarified butter. In Christian families a boy is baptised on the fortieth day and a girl on the eightieth, and at baptism the child receives a second, church name, such as Gabra Maryam, "servant of Mary". A cord called a mateb is tied around the baby's neck as the sign of baptism. Until then the baby is guarded from the evil eye and hardly ever taken outside.
primer.eth_p_childhood.title: Herd boys and the Psalter
primer.eth_p_childhood.text: A baby is carried on the back, tied on with a shawl. From five or six boys herd goats and calves and chase birds from the teff, while girls carry water in clay jars, gather dung for fuel and learn to grind grain. Priests' sons and the brightest children are sent to learn at the church: first the fidel syllabary, then the Psalms of David, sung by heart. Muslim children study the Quran with a sheikh. Punishment is strict, but godparents and uncles spoil the children with treats.
primer.eth_p_home.title: The tukul
primer.eth_p_home.text: A peasant's home is a tukul: a round hut of stone or of poles plastered with mud and straw, under a conical thatched roof. In Tigray people also build rectangular stone houses with flat roofs. A hearth burns in the middle, the smoke escapes through the thatch, and everything inside is black with soot. At night calves and goats sleep indoors to keep them safe from hyenas. There is hardly any furniture: hides on earthen benches, a woven basket-table called a mesob, clay pots and gourd flasks.
primer.eth_p_food.title: Injera and fasting
primer.eth_p_food.text: The staple is injera: large, slightly sour flatbreads made from teff, a tiny grain that grows almost nowhere else. On top goes wat, a thick stew of peas, lentils or meat with ginger, garlic and fragrant korarima, eaten by hand, tearing off pieces of bread. People drink tella, a barley beer, and tej, a honey wine served to nobles in horns. But devout Christians fast up to two hundred days a year: on Wednesdays, Fridays and through Lent they eat no meat, milk or eggs.
primer.eth_p_food_harar.title: Harar coffee
primer.eth_p_food_harar.text: Harar eats its own way: flatbreads of sorghum and wheat, meat with clarified butter, honey, and dates brought up from the coast. Pork and alcohol are forbidden to Muslims, so instead of tej people drink milk, honey water and, more and more, coffee: the bushes grow on the slopes around the city, and Sufis drink the hot brew at night prayers to stay awake. Nobody keeps the Christian fasts here, but during Ramadan the whole city goes without food from dawn to dusk and breaks the fast together at nightfall.
primer.eth_p_clothes.title: The white shamma
primer.eth_p_clothes.text: Men and women alike wear the shamma, a large white cotton wrap wound around the body and thrown over the shoulder; the way it is worn shows both your mood and your respect for the person you are talking to. Underneath, men wear knee-length trousers and women a long dress. People go barefoot. Nobles wear silk brought from India and Arabia and gold jewellery, and priests wear white turbans. Every baptised Christian has a mateb cord around the neck.
primer.eth_p_faith.title: Faith every day
primer.eth_p_faith.text: Most people here are Christians of the ancient Ethiopian Tewahedo Church. Alongside them live Muslims, in the east, in Harar and along the caravan routes, and the Beta Israel, the Jews of the northern mountains. In the south many honour a sky god and the spirits of the ancestors. Faith runs through every day: fasts, saints' days, prayers, oaths sworn in Mary's name. But rivalry between faiths is also one of the great driving forces of history here. Holy places are everywhere: a church on every hill, a monastery on every sheer mountain.
primer.eth_p_faith_tewahedo.title: Tabot and Ge'ez
primer.eth_p_faith_tewahedo.text: Your family belongs to the Ethiopian Tewahedo Church, "made one" in its faith in the single united nature of Christ. The head of the church, the abuna, is sent from Egypt, from Alexandria, and services are held in ancient Ge'ez, which ordinary people no longer understand. In many churches the holy of holies is hidden at the centre of a round building, and in it is kept the tabot, a tablet standing for the Ark of the Covenant. Following Zara Yaqob's ruling, both sabbaths are kept, Saturday and Sunday. Mary, Saint George and Takla Haymanot are especially beloved.
primer.eth_p_faith_islam.title: Islam in the highlands
primer.eth_p_faith_islam.text: Your family is Muslim. Islam came here very early: tradition says that in the Prophet Muhammad's own lifetime his persecuted companions found refuge with the king of Aksum. Muslims pray five times a day, fast in Ramadan, venerate the tombs of holy sheikhs and dream of making the pilgrimage across the Red Sea. Muslim merchants lead caravans all over the highlands, Christian lands included. But there is an age-old struggle with the Christian kingdom, and faith here is also a banner.
primer.eth_p_faith_judaism.title: Beta Israel
primer.eth_p_faith_judaism.text: Your family belongs to the Beta Israel, the "House of Israel", the Jews of the northern mountains. They honour the Torah in Ge'ez and strictly keep the Sabbath, the purity laws and the fasts; they have their own priests and even monks. They know nothing of the Talmud and have hardly heard of other Jews in the world. Christian kings have repeatedly made war on them and seized their land, and many Beta Israel, stripped of their fields, became smiths, potters and weavers. Neighbours call them Falasha, "strangers", with contempt, and fear them as sorcerers.
primer.eth_p_faith_traditional.title: The sky god
primer.eth_p_faith_traditional.text: Your family keeps the faith of the ancestors. Above everything is the sky god, whom the Oromo call Waaqa, and beneath him are the spirits of land, rivers, trees and forebears. Cattle are slaughtered for them, and milk and butter left at sacred trees and springs. Elders and ritual experts decide when to sow and how to make peace after a quarrel. Oromo life follows the gadaa system: every eight years power passes to a new generation of men. Christian monks come to convert people, but the old rites hold fast.
primer.eth_p_faith_catholic_early.title: The Catholics of Fremona
primer.eth_p_faith_catholic_early.text: Your family is Catholic, and there are few of them in the country: descendants of the Portuguese soldiers who came in 1541 to fight Gragn, their Ethiopian wives and converted neighbours. Since 1557 Jesuit missionaries led by Bishop Andrés de Oviedo have lived at Fremona, not far from Aksum. They say Mass in Latin, argue with local priests about the nature of Christ and hope to convert the king himself. The kings tolerate them, but ordinary believers look at them askance.
primer.eth_p_faith_catholic_late.title: The faith of Susenyos
primer.eth_p_faith_catholic_late.text: Your family has embraced Catholicism, the faith of the Portuguese Jesuits. In 1622 King Susenyos himself converted to the Roman faith, and Patriarch Afonso Mendes, who arrived in 1626, demanded that the people be rebaptised, the priests reordained, and the Saturday sabbath and ancient customs abolished. Many obeyed, but the country rose in revolt, and in 1632 the old faith was restored. The Jesuits were expelled, and those who remain Catholic had best keep quiet about it.
primer.eth_p_work.title: Salt instead of coins
primer.eth_p_work.text: Almost everyone here ploughs: oxen drag wooden ploughs across steep slopes where fields cling to stone terraces. There are hardly any coins. People pay in bars of salt, amole, carried by caravan from the Afar desert, and also in cloth, iron bars and gold dust. Craftsmen are needed by all, yet live apart. Merchants, mostly Muslims, lead mule caravans to the Red Sea with gold, ivory, civet musk and slaves, and bring back cloth, metal and spices.
primer.eth_p_place.title: The highlands
primer.eth_p_place.text: Your land is the Ethiopian highlands, a vast fortress of mountains and plateaus two to three kilometres high, slashed by gorges. It is cool here, and rain falls twice a year, while down in the hot lowlands lie deserts, malaria and foreign peoples. On flat-topped ambas, reached by a single path, people build monasteries, prisons and fortresses. The Blue Nile flows west out of these mountains, and legend says Egypt's very life depends on its waters.
primer.eth_p_place_lalibela.title: Churches in the rock
primer.eth_p_place_lalibela.text: Lalibela, once called Roha, is a town of eleven churches carved out of red volcanic rock. They were not built but cut from the top down: first a deep trench was hewn around a block of stone, then halls, windows and columns were hollowed out inside it. The cross-shaped church of Bete Giyorgis stands in a pit about twelve metres deep. The stream between the churches was named the Jordan. Legend says angels carried on the stonecutters' work by night, and on great feast days pilgrims gather here from all over the country.
primer.eth_p_place_aksum.title: City of the Ark
primer.eth_p_place_aksum.text: Aksum is the oldest and holiest city in the land. Above it stand the granite stelae of ancient kings, carved more than a thousand years ago; the largest, some thirty-three metres long, has lain broken on the ground for ages. The church of Mary of Zion is said to hold the Ark of the Covenant, brought here by Menelik, son of Solomon, and no one but its guardian may see it. Kings are crowned here: Zara Yaqob was crowned at Aksum in 1436. Women are not allowed onto the sacred ground of the church.
primer.eth_p_place_shewa.title: The royal camp
primer.eth_p_place_shewa.text: Shewa is a fertile plateau in the south of the kingdom and the heart of the Solomonic realm. Oxen plough the black soil, teff and barley grow, and cattle graze the high meadows. There is no fixed capital: the king roams with his camp of thousands of tents, and when the court halts near a village, its stores are eaten up within weeks. Here too stands the monastery of Debre Libanos, founded, tradition says, by Saint Takla Haymanot, and to the east, beyond the slopes, Muslim lands begin.
primer.eth_p_place_harar.title: City of saints
primer.eth_p_place_harar.text: Harar sits on the edge of the highlands where the roads to the sea, to Zeila and Berbera, meet. Its stone houses are whitewashed, its lanes so narrow that two donkeys cannot pass, and it has so many mosques and saints' tombs that it is called the city of saints. People here speak their own language, Harari, and write it in Arabic letters. The market sells cloth, salt, incense, coffee and, they say, leaves of khat, chewed to stay awake through night prayers.
primer.eth_p_law.title: A lawsuit in the open air
primer.eth_p_law.text: The highest judge is the king, and after him his governors and judges. Cases are argued in public, in the open air: plaintiff and defendant speak at length and with eloquence, trading proverbs, and each must name a guarantor who stakes his property on him. Judges rely on church rules and custom, and from the fifteenth or sixteenth century on the Fetha Nagast, "the Law of the Kings", a code translated from Arabic. Punishments include flogging, fines in cattle and cutting off a hand, with death for treason. Land disputes drag on for generations.
primer.eth_p_health.title: Holy water
primer.eth_p_health.text: The highlands protect people from the malaria that ravages the hot lowlands, but there are troubles enough up here: smallpox, typhus, leprosy, famine after drought or locusts. The sick are carried to holy springs, tsebel, where a priest pours blessed water over them. Learned church singers called debtera write prayers on long parchment scrolls and paint the faces of angels on them to ward off evil spirits. Healers treat the sick with herbs and cautery. The dead are buried by the church and remembered on the thirtieth and fortieth days.
primer.eth_p_women.title: Marriage and rist
primer.eth_p_women.text: Girls marry young, sometimes at twelve to fifteen, in matches arranged by their families. Most marriages are civil unions that can be dissolved by dividing the property; an indissoluble church wedding with communion is chosen by few, mainly priests. By custom daughters inherit rist on equal terms with sons, so a woman can own land and go to court over it. Women grind grain, bake injera, brew beer and spin cotton, while noble ladies, like Queen Eleni, govern and counsel kings.
primer.eth_p_women_harar.title: The women of Harar
primer.eth_p_women_harar.text: In Harar girls learn housekeeping and handicrafts early: Harari women are famous for woven baskets that hang on the walls of the home as the family's pride. Marriage follows Islamic law, the groom gives the bride a mahr, and a man may have up to four wives, though few can afford it. At home the woman is mistress, and many women trade in the market themselves. The most famous woman of Harar is Bati Del Wambara, wife of Imam Ahmad, who rode with him on campaign.
primer.eth_p_leisure.title: Timkat and Meskel
primer.eth_p_leisure.text: The great festivals belong to the church. At Timkat, Epiphany, in January, the tabots are carried to a river or pond, people sing all night, and in the morning the crowd is sprinkled with water. At Meskel, the Finding of the True Cross, in September as the rains end, huge bonfires are lit. At Christmas men and boys traditionally play genna, driving a wooden ball with hooked sticks. Nobles hold feasts with tej and horseback contests, and in the monasteries rings out the ancient chant attributed to Saint Yared.
primer.eth_p_knowledge.title: The Ge'ez script
primer.eth_p_knowledge.text: The country has an ancient script of its own, Ge'ez, in which every sign stands for a syllable, about two hundred signs in all. Books are written on goatskin parchment, bound between wooden boards and decorated with vivid miniatures. Monasteries are the centres of learning, where the Bible, saints' lives and royal chronicles are copied, and church chant and qene poetry with its double meanings, "wax and gold", are taught. Reading is mostly for priests, monks and debtera; for everyone else knowledge means proverbs, genealogies and tales.
primer.eth_p_war.title: An army on the march
primer.eth_p_war.text: The king's army is a whole city on the move: nobles bring their own men, infantry march with spears and hide shields, horsemen ride mules and horses, and behind them trail wives, servants and cattle. The army lives off the villages it passes through, and peasants fear it almost as much as an enemy. To the east lie the Muslim sultanates of Ifat and Adal, fought for centuries; to the south, pagan principalities. Every victory brings captives, cattle and new tribute.
primer.eth_p_war_guns.title: Guns and gadaa
primer.eth_p_war_guns.text: The war with Gragn showed what guns could do, and ever since the kings have obtained muskets from the Turks and the Portuguese and kept companies of musketeers, though powder and gunsmiths are always in short supply. Meanwhile the Oromo have been pushing up from the south since the 1520s: under the gadaa system, every eight years a new generation of warriors chooses a leader and sets out to win glory. Their cavalry is fast and their warriors tough. The kings must fight on several fronts at once, and many southern lands are lost to them.
